# Character Bible — *The Hour of Ash* (run 2)

> **Purpose.** The canonical home for the cast's VOICE and DISTINCTNESS, with one entry per NAMED
> character. This is a **living document**. The Architect seeded it in voice mode (2026-10-18), and the
> **Writer adds an entry the moment a new named character first appears on the page, before
> finalizing that chapter.** Dialogue Polish writes from these cards. The Evaluator and the Continuity
> Guardian audit against them. Facts and timeline live in `ENTITY_STATE.yaml`; the narration's voice and
> the anti-pattern budget live in `voice-dna.md`. This file is the per-character voice layer.
>
> **Sample lines are illustrations, not script.** Never paste one into the manuscript. The n-gram gates
> will flag it, and a line that appears here and on the page has become a catchphrase.

## How distinctness works here (read before adding a character)

Distinctness is **NOT** "give everyone a verbal tic." Characters are separated on **four axes**, in this
order of power:

1. **Attention / worldview:** what they NOTICE and reduce the world to. The deepest differentiator.
2. **Syntax / register:** sentence shape, clause habits, formality, questions against statements.
3. **Evasion:** what they will NOT say.
4. **Physicality / silence:** the body or the pause that stands in for speech.

There is no fifth thing. **Nobody has a verbal tic.** Each card also carries a **bleed guard**: what this
character must never borrow, usually from the narrator. When a narrator's habits leak onto the cast,
everyone starts to sound alike.

**Language on the page.** All speech is rendered in English, and the register signals the language.
Ancient speakers use no modern idiom and no modern units. Only Fenn, and Mara when she speaks English,
use modern idiom. See `voice-dna.md` §1, Dialogue conventions.

## Card format

```
#### [CHARACTER] — [role] (chapters)
- Attention / worldview:
- Vocabulary band:
- Syntax fingerprint:
- Rhythm:
- Evasion — never says:
- Physicality / silence:
- Verbal tic: none — distinguished by <axis>
- Bleed guard:
- Chaos on the page (subjects, never phrases):
- DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:
- Sample line:
```

---

## PRINCIPALS

### Voices from lives, not rules (author guard, 2026-10-24)
Every voice in this book comes from the person's life: background, work, wants, what they notice, what
they won't say, rhythm. Where a card records how a character compares things (Valens: never aloud;
Mara: freely, from 1998), that is a consequence written down so it does not drift, not a device. **From
Ch.26 on:** no new character is given an invented figurative habit or any other rule to fill a slot
(Philokrates, Secundus, Aelia and every walk-on are built from who they are); no one ever comments on
another character's habit; and the **nameable-rule test** applies at every evaluation: if a reader could
state a character's rule after one chapter ("he never…", "she always…"), it has become a gimmick and is
loosened toward the life it came from.

#### MARA REYES — narrator and protagonist; objects conservator, Philadelphia, b. 1965 (Ch.1–44)
- **Attention / worldview:** what a thing is made of, how it was joined, where it will fail and how it
  was mended. She reads people the same way: their hands, their teeth, the repaired places in them. She
  trusts what stays put (made things, the dead) and keeps a bag packed against what moves. **Only Mara
  notices materials and joins.**
- **Vocabulary band:** educated American, late-1990s frame of reference (answering machine, Pentax,
  Discman, payphones, SEPTA, Rite Aid, film sent away to develop), with nothing after spring 1998. Lab
  nouns leak in sparingly (squeeze-out, consolidant, chain lines, cold join, birch tar), never as a
  report form. She reads Attic Greek and Latin from books. Her spoken Greek begins as a classroom
  reconstruction that 1st-century ears find comic.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** **Narration:** long, clause-stacking sentences when interested, linked by
  semicolons and "and," with one sideways clause that comes back; plain short declaratives when afraid.
  **Speech:** quick and qualified, often answering a question with a question. In early Greek (Ch.4–10)
  her lines are short, careful and wrong. In Latin (Part Two) she is competent and accented. In English
  with Fenn she is fast, contracted and 1998. **As written in Ch.6 (synced 2026-10-19):** her Greek carries no
  contractions at all ("I shall not need to come down", "Had I any silver, you would have had silver", "Latin
  is not learned on this road"), so contractions mark her English ("They're fine."; the cliff speech; the
  plea to the rock). Her first Greek aloud in a month is to Valens in the lane.
- **Rhythm:** set chapter by chapter by the ledger's gear. Fragments are a pressure signal, so she
  rarely uses them in calm narration.
- **Evasion — never says:** the word *love* in her own narration until Part Two (first use no earlier
  than Ch.19, and rare after that); her father's death stated plainly (she circles it through his
  objects); any claim to be brave; any request to be looked after. After Ch.25 she will not put
  **Fenn's date** in the future tense (no "it will open in seventy-nine") until Ch.36. Hope for an
  earlier opening (Ch.30) and the argument over whether the door would take the children (Ch.33) are
  allowed; what she refuses is the date. She never says "Margaret" to Fenn.
- **Physicality / silence:** steady, competent hands that betray her only at thresholds. She **touches
  surfaces to read them** (a thumbnail along a seam, a fingertip on a glaze, her palm on painted
  plaster). When she cannot speak she *inspects* something. Under pressure her hands act neatly by
  themselves (sample-05).
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (materials and joins) and syntax (spiral in
  interest, clip in fear)
- **Bleed guard:** her dry asides and her eye for materials must never migrate into anyone else's
  dialogue. Avoid "the conservator in me" as a recurring phrase (at-risk list).
- **Chaos on the page (subjects, never phrases):** **teeth** (full surfacings Ch.7, 20, 31; glancing
  only in Ch.2 floss, Ch.5 Kallia inspects hers, Ch.15 Valens's, Ch.24 the midwife's. **Ch.15: DONE, glancing** (SYNCED 2026-10-20 to the
  FINAL page): Valens's teeth seen ("His teeth showed by the doorway's glow, square and even."), held against him by her own record ("I
  had flossed every night of my adult life and still paid to be scolded twice a year"), in "the wreck of the herdsman's bed"; the dentist
  is unnamed and has no costume. **Teeth fact:** "every night" sits inside foundation's twice a day, and no later page states another
  frequency. The floss itself last appears in Ch.5 (the old filling "that frayed the floss"); from Ch.7 she cleans her teeth with a
  lentisk stick, so no later page shows her using 1998 floss in antiquity unless it accounts for it (how much is left, where it is
  kept). "every night of my adult life" is the habit of her 1998 life; it does not claim she has flossed this year. The Ch.24
  midwife is still the book's only introduction-by-teeth; the Ch.24
  midwife is the book's only introduction-by-teeth, and the rule stays at most one in any four chapters).
  **All-or-nothing** (Ch.1, 5, 7, 9, 20, 29, 33; the ending must read as accepting a seam, not as this
  distortion). **Mrs. Dunphy** (Ch.7 green cardigan; Ch.24 brown; Ch.41 unsure it was long division).
  **Mundane breaks** (Ch.6 the scream, Ch.20 the pebble, Ch.22 the sneeze).
- **CONTINUITY COMMITMENT (from late Ch.7, ¶378; logged 2026-10-19 from the Ch.7 re-evaluation):** "from the
  next night I kept even my own company in Greek." From that night on, Mara does **not speak English to
  herself**: no muttered English, no English said aloud alone in the dark, no English prayer or curse under
  her breath, and no English address or name recited to keep it. **English to a listener does not break it:**
  her English with Fenn (Ch.25 on) is speech to another person. Any later solitary English must be written as
  a **deliberate, visible break** of this commitment, and the page should register it as one. (Her English
  *thoughts* are the narration itself and are not affected.) The commitment is her all-or-nothing distortion
  escalating inside one chapter (¶148 public silence → ¶378 private English); the beat of renouncing a register
  is SPENT after these two (see at-risk after Ch.7, cycle 1).

#### VALENS ("Lupus") — muleteer, former murmillo, freedman; b. c. AD 38 in Thrace (Ch.6–44)
- **Attention / worldview:** footing, exits, weather, and the moods of animals and men, which are one
  skill to him. He reads bodies before faces and asks who saw. His worldview: whoever is close enough
  to know you is close enough to sell you, so be useful and be nobody.
- **Vocabulary band:** Latin-plain, arena and road register; concrete nouns (ground, rope, hoof, gate,
  bread, ship, weight, rain). **No abstractions in his mouth:** never honor, destiny, justice or fate.
  In Greek (Part One) he is flatly literal, without idiom, using a tool he never learned to enjoy. In
  Latin (Part Two) he is a shade looser and allows himself a dry understatement. His Thracian childhood
  surfaces only as the onion memory, never as words.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** short, level declaratives. He rarely subordinates, and **never uses a simile
  or comparison in speech.** His questions are practical (where, how far, how heavy, who saw). He asks
  *why* only of plans, never of feelings. He understates danger to almost nothing.
- **Rhythm:** statements in ones and twos with silence between. His longest speeches are evidence given
  in strict chronological order (the telling at the stream, Ch.12; the testimony, Ch.22): a witness, not
  a reflective man. **In Ch.34 alone he talks freely and at length.** That is how ease sounds in him.
- **Evasion — never says:** anything about the men he killed; that he is afraid; the word *love* until
  it is said once, plainly, in Ch.43; any grievance about the frame; any request that Mara stay.
- **Physicality / silence:** stillness. When a conversation comes too close he finds maintenance work
  for his hands, and **it is always a different object** (a hoof, a girth strap, a lamp wick, a knife
  edge, the potted fig, a child's sandal strap). It is never a fixed gesture and never ends a scene. He
  is enormously careful with small objects (the watch) and gentle with animals and children. He hands the
  chicken to someone else.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (footing, bodies, animals) and syntax (short, level,
  unsubordinated, no comparisons)
- **Bleed guard:** must never notice materials or workmanship the way Mara does. When he admires the
  watch, it is as a well-made *working* thing ("It's alive"), not as craft. No wry asides.
- **Chaos on the page (subjects, never phrases):** **figs** (Ch.11, 20, 34; spent after that).
  **Mind-reading threat** (Ch.6, 11, 19, 21, 28, 37: he is wrong in mundane ways). **Onion memory**
  (Ch.12, 22, 23, 32, 41; never explained). **The mime** (Ch.29: he weeps at a farce).
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the only speaker who never compares one thing to another and never asks why
  about a feeling, against Mara, whose every other sentence qualifies, compares or asks.
- **Why he talks this way (the life, not a rule — author guard, 2026-10-24):** a slave taken as a boy,
  trained to fight, kept alive by reading ground, distance and men's bodies exactly as they are. A man
  who has bet his life on what is literally in front of him has no use for "like". The plainness is who
  he is; it is NOT a device. **So:** nobody ever remarks on it (no "you never say what anything is like"),
  no line is built to show it off, and it is never staged as a joke or a reveal. Ordinary dead idiom a
  muleteer would use without hearing it as a figure is allowed and should not be policed out. If the
  absence ever starts to read as a gimmick, loosen it toward the man, never add a new rule.
- **Sample line:** "He's lame in the off hind. Not your doing. Hold his head and keep talking to him; he
  likes your voice."
- **Ch.6 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; first live appearance, Delphi and Parnassus, November AD 70. SYNCED to
  the final page 2026-10-19, after dialogue-polish, disruptor, continuity repair and polish cycle 1. Every quote
  below is on the page, except the cut wordings named as cut in the recast notes):**
  **Body (the page's only body facts):** a scar the length of Mara's finger across the back of his **right**
  hand; whoever closed it was in a hurry and set the stitches too far apart, and it healed "in a ladder, every
  rung raised and white" (Mara's repairer's eye, not his). When he leans on the gray's shoulder, "she had to brace
  a foot under his weight" (size), and his scarred hand "was an older hand than the rest of him" (wear; both read by Mara; no face, eyes,
  teeth or beauty word anywhere in the chapter; his ~32 stays unstated). His thumb covers the watch's crown
  entirely; the band will not go halfway round his wrist, so the watch lives in his belt pouch. Later chapters
  give new body facts in fresh words; do not re-quote the ladder or the hands sentence.
  **Entry behavior:** stops his string short of Kallia's gate and walks the iced lane alone, looking at the
  ground; then to Mara, a woman in a gateway with a jar: "Ashes. For the ice. Before they come up." Throws them in
  low, flat fans where a hoof will come down, and brings the mules up singly. Mara learns his name from Kallia
  ("Not in my court, Valens"). He never asks hers ("No."). Sells Kallia split oak ("Split this month. It'll
  burn." / "That was pine. This is oak." / "Five. It's oak."), answers her fast Phocian "a word at a time" and
  gives one coin back; to her questions: "The last ship went out of Kirrha eight days ago." / "Oil. Wine from
  Crete. A man with dogs to sell." / "I don't carry letters." Of Mara's crosswise woodstack: "Who showed you
  that?" (whether a load stands: his axis, not workmanship).
  **Syntax and register as written:** plain, contracted Greek, spoken "slowly and flatly, every ending in its
  place"; Mara follows all of it (and loses the charcoal burner), against her uncontracted book Greek. Short level
  declaratives in ones and twos, almost no subordination. Questions practical only: "Pan's cave. What's up
  there?" / "With what?" / "How long is that?" / "How long does it go?" / "And if a man forgets?" / "And when it's
  tight?" / "Who makes them?" / "For hire?" / "What stops it rocking?" His one *why* is of a plan ("Why tomorrow?
  It'll be there in the spring."). He reckons time and risk in his own consumables: her "until the long hand is at
  the eight" becomes "Most of a pine, then"; "Two more pines after this one"; "I'm paid for the down as well as
  the up." **No comparison or simile in his speech:** dialogue-polish recast "like a book" as "You talk a
  schoolmaster's Greek." and "like the stones in the sanctuary" as "You read the letters on the rock without
  spelling them out."; the writer recast "longer" as "a morning and more". Bleed watch (eval #16): "The widow
  carries her own water again." / "It's his. Whoever goes up in the spring." lean into Kallia's who-pays-the-labor
  axis; from Ch.7 to Ch.12 he reckons in ground, bodies and animals, and Kallia in labor.
  **Attention on the page:** ice and ashes; the stair ("The stair's ice from the second turn"); sacking bound on
  the hooves with the twine pulled tight in his teeth (on the cliff, and fresh at the kiln); the ground under the
  snow read by the lie of the walls and the tops of the thornbushes; the crust tried with his heel before he
  trusts it; the buried ditch; the weather ("There's snow coming over the ridge"; "Snow by afternoon"); a man with
  a donkey on the path below, watched through two turns and then three; her hands ("Those never carried a jar
  till this month."); and what he hears in the dark (her two trips to the spring before they left). Footing
  orders, each caused by terrain on the page: "Hold that. She'll pull." / "Step where she steps. Not where I
  step." / "Sit back. Hold the saddle, not her mouth. Let her find it." / "Ditch." / "Keep to the wall. The edge
  has gone along this bit." Of her English talk on the cliff he catches only "Philadelphia" ("There's a
  Philadelphia in Asia. … Past Sardis. A man I knew came from there." / "Past Asia there's only Parthians.").
  **Mind-reading (wrong in mundane ways):** the donkey man is "Somebody for you" (a charcoal burner); she was
  digging for "Silver. Whatever you ran with."; and the long reading on the last descent, given with his back to
  her: "He'll have you all over the town by the next market. … So here's what I make of you." In order: down off
  the top in the autumn, by herself, in trousers; hands that never worked; the letters on the rock read without
  spelling; "You've got Latin" (his second use; cap reached); a thing on her wrist "no smith in Achaea could
  make"; no name, hers or her people's. "That's a big house. Corinth, or Patrae. Somebody there wants you back, a
  father or a husband, and whoever he is, he's got the money to look. And there's one man in Delphi who'd take a
  mule up Parnassus in the snow." The close is self-exposure, not prediction: the fear underneath is his own
  traceability, and he says nothing about anyone coming. Mara: "Most of it was true, and the whole of it was
  wrong."
  **The watch:** taken as payment the evening before ("Paid now. Not up there. Now."). "He was a long while over
  the back of it, and over the band where the three links had come out"; he watches the seconds hand make one
  circuit with his face unchanged ("Something's going in it." / "Where's the shadow?" / "By itself."). Winds it
  BACKWARD with great care, his thumb covering the crown, stopping to listen to the loose click "as if the click
  were what it was for"; Mara lets him turn it twice more before she can say stop, gives it three turns forward,
  and he finishes until the crown pushes back. "I won't drop it." In the cave he shows her the dial on his palm
  without handing it over (twice) and closes his fingers over it at five to two. Refuses to sell it back ("The
  watch." / "It's a good watch." / "You paid it to go up. You went up." / "You said he didn't need it."). Repeats
  her rule once: "Forward. Till it stops, and not past." (There is no "Not past" exchange; dialogue-polish cut the
  three-line antiphon.)
  **The coin:** pinches her 50-drachma piece off her palm (brass, an old bearded head; Mara: "A poet.") and returns
  it: "That buys nothing up there. Or down here."
  **Mules:** unnamed (the gray, the brown that ate Kallia's pomegranate last winter, a dun): "A name's for calling.
  They come when they see the barley bag." Talks to them low in Latin (*Ambula, asini filia*): "They came from
  Corinth. They don't know any Greek." … "These know Latin."
  **Pan and the cave:** leaves a corner of crust on the ledge ("It's his house." / "I pay him." / "It's what I
  do."); asks what the inscription says and answers "That's what the goat boys say it says" (he does not admit to
  reading). Makes fire slowly with steel, flint and bracket fungus ("No."). Holds each pine off to one side so
  that his shadow falls away from her work; lights the next from the stub and grinds the stub out under his boot.
  **The laugh and the bread:** once, at her scream: "short and surprised, and ran on briefly after, a laugh with
  nobody at the end of it" (cycle 1 cut the sentence comparing it to the Sacred Way laugh). "Good." The bread from
  the front of his tunic, broken across his knee, warm. "He finished what was in his mouth first." / "It was the
  first thing you did up here I understood." / "A thief doesn't fill the widow's jar before she goes."
  **Looking after her without saying so (the descent):** "Where do you sleep?" / "Dry?" / "Does she hit you?" /
  "She feeds you." / "Stay where you are. She'll keep you while you work."
  **Evasions on the page:** where he's from ("North."); where he learned Latin ("On the road."; Mara: "Latin is
  not learned on this road."); her name (never asked); her story ("Don't.", then "Keep to the wall…", the refusal
  done as footing). Would have walked past the kiln; the gray turned for the warmth. Lies smoothly for her there
  ("She's the widow Kallia's. Down by the spring." / "Since the olives." / "She came off a ship." / "She hit
  Pan.").
  **Hands:** all his maintenance business in Ch.6 is mule tack (girths, a lead tied into a tail, sacking,
  unlashing). Vary the object class from Ch.7 (audit N-16: a knife edge, a lamp wick, a sandal strap).
  **Last line:** gives her the duffel, then the shovel: "Men will come asking. You went up by yourself. You never
  had a watch." The threat is spoken once, here, as the pull.
  **Spent in Ch.6 (do not reuse):** the backward winding (every later winding is forward and worded fresh);
  "Something's going in it"; "Where's the shadow?"; "It's his house" / "I pay him"; "A name's for calling";
  "These know Latin"; "He's cheap"; "Good." after the scream; "a laugh with nobody at the end of it"; "It was the
  first thing you did up here I understood."; "Most of a pine, then"; "So here's what I make of you." and the
  evidence-in-order reading; "one man in Delphi who'd take a mule up Parnassus in the snow"; "Keep to the wall.
  The edge has gone along this bit."; "You've got Latin" (2, cap reached); "Men will come asking" (once, the
  pull); "You never had a watch"; "Forward. Till it stops, and not past."; "his hands were older than the rest of
  him"; the scar "in a ladder".

- **Ch.7 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; brief, the middle of her month of public silence. SYNCED to the final page
  2026-10-19, after dialogue-polish, disruptor, continuity repair, polish cycle 1 and the three finalize fixes; every
  quote below is on the page, checked by script):** comes to
  Kallia's gate with the mules for the fifth coin. Mara, in her month of public silence and taught to look at men's
  feet, sees ONLY his boots (rawhide, laced to the shin, one lace broken and knotted). Lines: "It burned." / "Oak
  doesn't spit." / to Mara: "She's taught you to walk," / "You've stopped talking." / to Kallia's "She's simple": "No."
  Leaves without the coin (Kallia: "Once on my good hearthstone and once in the lentils."). No hands, no face, no
  romance signal; Mara wonders only whether he wound the watch before he saw to the mules or after, "and whether he
  remembered which way". His boat lie to the burner has become Mara's legal story (Kallia adds Syracuse). He still
  does not know her name. Spent: the boots-only sighting; "No." as his whole answer to a claim about her; the
  spitting-oak exchange (see at-risk after Ch.7: the fifth coin is settled off the page).

- **Ch.8 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; one glimpse only, no line. SYNCED to the final page 2026-10-19):** at the
  corner of "the last roof in Delphi" (a long low building with a stable at one end), where the men stop, holding the
  gray by her headstall with her face turned in to the stable wall "so that the torches would not set her off"; "he had
  his own back to us as well, like every man who had come that far" (the logic fix: the men in the street had been
  watching). Mara knows him by the mule ("It was the gray, so it was Valens") and sees only "the mule's ears go back and

- **Ch.9 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; the eval's escalation met: one spoken exchange, practical, before the notice.
  SYNCED to the final page 2026-10-19, after dialogue-polish, disruptor, continuity repair, polish cycle 1 and the bending fix;
  every quote below is on the page, checked by script):** "At the back gate Valens was unloading split wood off a line of mules
  into the priest's woodshed." The gray is tied apart with her load off, a pot of pitch hung on the gatepost; he works it into a
  saddle gall on her withers. "Her ears were flat. When she swung her head round to bite him he put her nose away with his elbow
  and went on working." (the disruptor cut the two-fingered caress as a romance cue: do not restore it). Lines: "For her back.
  The new saddle's rubbed her." (one speech) / "What for?" / "That's the god's," / "Will it stand?" / "Somebody will." / "An
  obol." / "He'll pay." (dialogue-polish cut "Warm it first…" as his spent order-plus-consequence shape and a bleed into Mara's
  materials axis.) Attention: before answering, "His eyes left me for the court: to the stand on its sack in the sun, and to the
  old man on his basket by the hives, who had gone to sleep sitting up." (who is watching). "He wiped his fingers on the gray's
  mane, unhooked the pot and broke the cake of pitch in it with the haft of his knife"; the pitch is "almost black, cold and
  brittle, with a mule hair in it." "He bent to her withers again." (the "[S] bent to [the X] again" frame is CLOSED: see at-risk
  after Ch.9). Still does not know her name; no romance signal; no closeness, so no practical-order deflection. **The notice (no
  words on either side):** he comes into the square at its upper corner "with the gray behind him on a slack rope. She carried
  nothing."; "at his ordinary pace"; "He halted at the board."; stands "while a slow man might read it once, and then as long
  again" (the page does not confirm that he reads; Ch.11 keeps that reveal); "He turned his head and found me there by the
  column."; "He looked back at me while a cart came in at the top of the square and rolled down past us"; takes the gray "down
  the square at a walk, past the men still at the eel-seller, to the trough below the fountain"; last line: "He let the gray
  drink first." Nobody in Delphi calls him Lupus; the men at the board joke about the name without connecting it to him (the
  Hostile reader's open question for Ch.10–11: a scarred Thracian at the board in daylight, unconnected by five men). His
  "How long…?" stays at 3 book-wide (all Ch.6). Spent: the pitch exchange; "He'll pay."; "Somebody will."; the silent look at
  the board; letting the gray drink first; the bite elbowed away.

- **Ch.11 as written (Writer, 2026-10-20; the full two-hander of AUTHOR-CP2-1, scene after scene. SYNCED to the FINAL page
  2026-10-20, after dialogue-polish, hook-craft, the disruptor, continuity repair, polish cycle 1 and finalize lines F1, F3, F4;

  out the obol: "He took it and tucked it into his cheek, the way the men did in the market when their hands were full." ("The obol
  made a small lump in his cheek when he talked.") **New body fact (fresh words next time; do not re-quote):** "Close to, a white
  nick ran through one eyebrow, across the grain of the hair."; he tries the knife on his forearm "and it took the hair off clean". At
  the near-kiss: "The nick in his eyebrow showed." **The broken nose is CUT** (polish cycle 1: it was Nikaso's Ch.8 introduction;
  CLOSED for every later face). **The refusal, as crowd-reading, not fear, with no bare "No.":** to her ask, "He kept the stone

  god's first day the whole sanctuary's full. Every man in Phocis with a question, all of them watching each other. A priest writes

  board, with the pretence that he cannot read: "I heard it read out." / "Whoever stood by it. There's always one." / "He started on

  you let it stop?": "He loosened the drawstring of his belt pouch with a finger, looked into it, and left the watch where it was." /
  "The short one's past the nine," … "The long one's at the two." It is fast by the spout's shadow; "Since the mountain he had kept it
  going, every day, and he had not put a finger to the hands." / "It hasn't stopped." He pulled the pouch shut. (Felix: "Each day
  before he's had his bread he does something to it, with his back to me".) **The breeching:** "It's been breaking all winter." / "I
  never asked for it mended." / "He sheathed the knife at his back and crossed to the stable."; the load test, "over the beam it went,
  and with an end in each fist he hung his whole weight from it, his feet off the cobbles. The beam creaked, and the strap held." /
  "I did. At Kirrha, by a fire." / he hangs it "on its peg himself" / "There's a heap more under that bench." **The awl (no
  subject):** "In the morning the awl lay on the bench beside the girth, and somebody had put a point on it that would have gone
  through a sole." **Hands on new object classes, never tack as a frame:** whetstone and knife; the obol; the load test; the mules'
  bells stuffed with wool; the lame black's hoof; the bran sack; **a boot lace** ("he stayed, with a foot up on the bench, to put a
  new lace in his boot" / "He ran the lace on up the shin and tucked the end in."; Ch.7's broken, knotted lace replaced, never
  pointed at; the struck KNOT is gone, and F1 cut the clause that stopped the lace at the freedom question); the lamp wick ("pinched
  off the char with his fingers"); two stones set back in the goats' gap; the sack eased "out of his hand without hurry". **The four
  reveals, in the outline's order:** (1) **figs**, his chaos trait's first surfacing: "They're Caunian. They're meant to be like
  that." / "A fig that gives has gone to the wasps." / "You pick when the skin splits by itself. A day in the shade first, on the
  tree's own leaves. After that the sun, whole, on a rush, turned every morning, and in at nightfall, ahead of the dew." / "Where's
  that?" / "They don't, in Syracuse." / "Split, the dust gets in," … "come the spring you've a jar of mold." / "Pressed, they're a

  who've never had a Caunian." / "That one's Caunian." (pointing "with the half fig at the tree in its jar") / "From a cutting. In a

  / to "Somebody else would have to open mine,": "Then I'm right." (2) **the lame black:** "Again," / "Near fore,"; he "laid his hand
  flat on her shoulder and ran it down the leg, slowly, to the fetlock"; to the twitch, no line: "Valens was watching the hoof, and

  "Bran," … "Hot." / "She'd remember it." / "That's why."; up all night (Felix: "There's three sacks gone, and I never heard him

  stayed off the sherd." / "Ask for a road. A road they'll answer." / "It was on the bench." / "I did hear it." Then, to Felix's "Read

- **The legal claim as the page now has it (continuity W-21; the prose wins over foundation §3):** the freedom WAS registered: "I put
  the Gaul down, and he sent the sword out to me across the sand, and a magistrate wrote my name in his book." The registration is not
  in dispute. Celer's claim is a prior sale: "His story was that he'd bought me from the lanista the month before the games, so the
  lanista had no right to free me, and the magistrate had written down a mistake. So I was his." In plot terms Celer's case rests on a
  backdated bill of sale. The words "bill of sale" and "backdated" are NOT on the page; Valens says only "His story was". **Consequence
  for Ch.15, 17 and 22:** the Corinth record proves the lanista freed him before witnesses and the emperor, but on its own it no longer
  refutes Celer. The Rome suit has to defeat the sale itself: the lanista's books, the date, or the fact that Celer hired him for wages
  after the games ("After the sword I needed work. Celer" … "wanted a man to walk behind his wife"). Valens never argues the law; he
  gives the chronology and stops. (Foundation §3's "never registered before a magistrate" and the Ch.17/Ch.22 outline beats still carry
  the old claim: flagged for the architect/orchestrator, not patched in this file.)

#### AUGUST FENN / "AUGURINUS" — the vanished treasure hunter; b. 1934 Philadelphia; crossed 1968, landed AD 41; Puteoli astrologer (documents Ch.2; in person Ch.25–35; dies winter 78–79)
- **Attention / worldview:** systems and patterns: tides, tremors, star tables, the doors' timing, box
  scores. **He sees people last.** His worldview: his real life is the one he is going back to. He has
  never furnished a room here.
- **Vocabulary band:** **in English, frozen in 1968** (see the pool below), with Navy and treasure-hunter
  bravado and Philadelphia vowels. **In Greek, perfect, formal and courtly** after more than three decades. He
  is the only character whose second language is better than his first is current. His English documents
  move from boyish capitals (1967) to small, tired script (1968).
- **Syntax fingerprint:** **excited:** runaway sentences chained on "and," changing subject mid-stream and
  correcting himself ("No, don't tell me"). **Tired:** four-word fragments. **No enumerating, numbering or
  listing habit, ever** (struck by the no-tics law). His pattern-mind shows in *what he talks about*,
  never in a verbal device.
- **Rhythm:** bursts and collapses; asks questions and refuses the answers.
- **Evasion — never says:** his sister's name in person until Ch.35 (his 1968 notebook names Margaret
  freely; the silence grew over the decades). In Ch.25 "estate sale" tells him she is dead, and he does

## MAJOR SECONDARIES

#### KALLIA — widow who keeps a pilgrims' lodging by the Castalian spring, Delphi (Ch.5–16; farewell Ch.16)
- **Attention / worldview:** **costs in labor:** who carries the water, who will clean it, how many
  hands a thing takes. The world is chores and the people who do them.
- **Vocabulary band:** Phocian village Greek; household nouns (jar, broom, wool, hearth, beans, pilgrims,
  rent). Nothing learned and nothing quoted (**no proverbs**: struck).
- **Syntax fingerprint:** short imperatives. **She answers a question with a task** (CAPPED from Ch.10 at **1 chore-reply
  per chapter**, and sending someone off on an errand instead of answering counts as the same device; her other replies
  are silence, an act, a question back or a flat fact: see at-risk after Ch.10 FINAL). Her own questions
  are practical (can you carry water, can you card wool, is she Greek, can she weave), and under them sits
  the question she cannot ask.
- **Rhythm:** few words, then work. She never finishes a speech; she goes and does something instead.
- **Evasion — never says:** her son's name, until the letter forces it once (Ch.10); anything about
  herself or her widowhood; thanks; goodbye (Ch.16 is a sweep and a put-away broom, no speech).
- **Physicality / silence:** **never sits** while anyone else is working. Always something in her hands.
  She touches objects, not people (contrast Grata). The broom laid across the empty room's threshold.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (labor and its cost) and evasion (never speaks of
  herself)
- **Bleed guard:** never notices how a thing is *made* (Mara's); only who has to *do* it.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the woman who replies to every question with a job, against Theano, who
  replies to every question with a complaint about herself.
- **Sample line:** "Water first. Cry after. The jar's by the door and the spring won't come to you."
- **Ch.5 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; first live appearance):** about fifty; broad brown face lined
  across the forehead; gray hair dragged back under a dark kerchief. Comes to the Castalian spring after
  dark with a jar on her head and a lamp in her hand, to fill the jar (the page says only "a lamp", no
  material; it gives no reason beyond the errand).
  Her lodging is a short walk above the spring, up the road and along a lane ("near" the spring, not
  beside the basin). **Her own life before
  she sees Mara:** fishes a pilgrims' limp garland out of the basin and flings it down the slope
  ("Boeotians"), then washes each foot under the overflow with her eyes shut. Lines are imperatives and
  practical questions only: "Out of the basin. People drink that." / "Who beat you?" / "Hands." / "Turn
  them." / "Open your mouth." / "What's that? Lead?" (Mara's amalgam filling) / "Who saw you come down
  here?" / "Can you carry water? … card wool? Weave? Grind? Cook?" / "Whose are you?" / "Bring the jar."
  She **never touches Mara**: she inspects hands and teeth by lamplight and demonstrates opening her own
  mouth and carrying on the head. Answers Mara's long English outburst by pointing at the jar (a task).
  The one sentence about her household, not herself: "I've a houseful of Thebans, and the girl ran off
  at the vintage." On the way home she bangs up a neighbor at night to reclaim her fine horsehair sieve
  (lent "a month" ago for the neighbor's wife to strain her must; it comes back with a hole; she threatens to shame the wife at the spring).
  Mara answers her in English throughout, or by a head-shake (the Greek refusal holds from the
  guide's mimicry on); Kallia reads tone, not words ("Mine." is said in English). Her name reaches Mara only when a pilgrim shouts it from the gallery; to "Who's that you've got?" she
  says "A pair of hands" and, to "Can she sing?", "She can carry." Work orders: ashes out before light,
  hearth swept, two jars from the spring before the pilgrims wake, then the floors and the Thebans' pots.
  "Don't touch the oil." Takes the lamp away (lamp oil is lamp oil); later throws a goat-hair blanket in
  from the dark ("Blanket"). **She never asks Mara's name.** No thanks, no sitting, no proverb, no
  speech about herself. Her son's room is NOT shown (held for Ch.7).
- **Ch.6 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; backfill, the afternoon and night before the climb):** buys a string of
  split oak from Valens in the lane. Her own life, not Mara's: stands with her back to the pomegranate trunk, arms
  crooked out, to keep the gray mule out of her court ("She had that tree to the height of her head last winter");
  smells the cut end of a split ("Wet." / "It'll spit. The last lot spat a coal on a Theban's cloak, and I paid for
  the cloak." / "Then it'll spit oak."); haggles ("Four now, and the fifth when I've seen it burn without
  spitting"); pays from a knot in her kerchief corner, then goes at him in Phocian too fast for Mara to follow
  (he answers a word at a time) until he gives her one coin back, and ties the knot up again more slowly than she
  untied it. (Synced to the final page 2026-10-19; every other quote in this block is on the page.) Asks Valens whether the
  sea is shut and whether anything came in from the east before the last ship left Kirrha, then "Letters." /
  "Nobody asked what you carry." (her son; unexplained on the page). Of Mara: "Don't wait for an answer. She
  doesn't talk." Orders: "You. Under the stair. Bark up." To a Theban on the gallery: "When the hearth comes."
  That night, from the dark at the top of the outside stair as Mara leaves with the duffel and her ash shovel:
  "The shovel comes back." Mara thanks her for the blanket in English; Kallia: "Shut the gate behind you." Still
  never touches Mara, never asks her name, never speaks of herself.

  / "She came on one of the last boats, after the vintage." / "Half Syracuse is Roman," / "I do." / "Who stands for my

#### THEANO — the Pythia; a farmer's widow off duty (glimpsed Ch.8 unnamed, shouting at crows; Ch.13)
- **Attention / worldview:** her own body (her knees, the descent into the adyton), the priests' petty
  politics, the crows. She treats the god like a difficult employer and the oracle like a job with bad
  conditions.
- **Vocabulary band:** plain mountain Phocian Greek, a farmer's widow's words. **No oracular verse, no
  riddles, no portent**, except when she repeats the god's public answer, which is *his* language and not
  hers.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** grumbling run-on complaint, then a flat fact delivered with no softening.
- **Fact:** she goes down into the adyton on the monthly consultation days of the warm season. In Ch.13
  she takes Mara's last two ibuprofen for her knees without thanks. She
  refuses questions or answers them in one word.
- **Rhythm:** a long complaint, then a short answer, then a return to the complaint.
- **Evasion — never says:** anything comforting; any explanation of the god, the answer or the hour (she
  explains herself once, about the crows, Ch.13: "Because they come." … "A thing that'll sit quiet at a
  burying can have my barley."; continuity W-13 / ENTITY CH13-13, card amended 2026-10-20); any hint of
  the hour. Whether the hour is "not hers to give" or "not given," she will not say which.
- **Physicality / silence:** sits whenever she can. Her knees are what she talks about, not a gesture she
  repeats: one knee beat per appearance (Ch.8 "She kept her free hand on her knee the whole time"; Ch.13
  "She pressed her knees with the heels of her hands."); a return gets a new beat or none. Feeds the
  crows the god's barley, shouts at them for taking it, and lies about it.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (her body and her grievances) and evasion (no
  comfort; no explanation of the god or the hour)
- **Bleed guard:** must not sound like Kallia (see the guarantee) or like a fantasy oracle.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the only character who talks freely about herself and gives nothing away,
  against Kallia, who gives a stranger a roof and never says a word about herself.
- **Sample line:** "Once a month all summer that god has me down a hole on these knees, and those men won't
  spare me a stool. Well? Ask it. It's going to rain."

- **Ch.8 as written (Writer, 2026-10-19; UNNAMED, unrecognised, texture only. SYNCED to the final page 2026-10-19 after
  continuity W-05/W-15):** an old woman on a block of stone by her door at the last gate but one, a basket of barley in
  her lap, throwing it "over the frozen ruts a fistful at a time" to the crows ("black on the white rime, walking about
  with their shoulders up") and shouting at them for taking it: "Black thieves," … "every one of you. That's not for
  you." / "Go on, then. Take it. Choke on it." "She kept her free hand on her knee the whole time, and her eyes on the
  crows." (The draft's clause about whose barley it was and the no-look sentences were cut: no wink.) Nobody names her or explains her.
  Ch.13 recognises her by situation only (the crows); do not re-quote these lines there.
- **Ch.13 as written (Writer, 2026-10-20; FIRST LIVE APPEARANCE AND NAMED. SYNCED to the FINAL page 2026-10-20, polish cycle 1 + FZ1–FZ3;
  every quote below is on the page, checked by script):** **Seen unrecognized at dawn:** "old, and veiled to the eyes in white wool, with a
  sprig of laurel in her hand", led up the ramp by two priests "at the pace of her slowest foot", halting on every temple step "while she
  brought her second foot up beside the first" (a walk-on: "That's her," … "She'll be going down now."). **Named by the jug boy** ("Theano
  wants her.") and by Kallia ("The god's woman," … "She'll have you carry her water up while you're there. She does that." Theano does not).
  **Recognized by situation only (CH8-2):** "the house next to the highest", a squared stone at the door "gone round at the corners with
  being sat on", "a dozen crows waited in a row", parched barley flung "over the ruts"; no Ch.8 line re-quoted (her new scolding: "Look at
  that," … "Robbers. The minute a woman sits down." / "Get off, you, you've had yours."). **One knee beat:** "She pressed her knees with the
  heels of her hands." **Body:** "a farmer's hands, square, the nails broken short, and a face the sun had burned brown and crumpled under

  grievances (she talks freely about herself):** the stool ("not a man of them will carry a stool down after me. They've stools; they've a
  stool for the square beard" … "They said they'd put it to the council. The council! For a stool!"); her husband who "dragged this stone
  here for me before he died" … "with two oxen and a lever and a deal of cursing"; "Listen to them. You can hear them from there, can't
  you?" (Mara cannot); "Down," … "Up, I can lean on the wall."; "Fourteen years I've had that god, since my husband went" (Pythia after
  widowhood, over fifty at selection); "When I started there were three of us to take turns" … "Now there's only me"; her sister's son keeps

  … "They were up on that ridge the day my husband went out of this door feet first, the whole row of them, and not a crow of them made a
  sound, which the mourners never managed. A thing that'll sit quiet at a burying can have my barley." She explains nothing of the god, the
  answer or the hour. **The ibuprofen (one beat):** "What's that?" / she "took them off my palm with two fingers", "put both pills in her
  mouth at once, drank from the cup and swallowed, wiped her mouth on the back of her wrist", no thanks, another fistful at the crows; never
  mentioned again. **She heard the carrier from below:** "shifting about over your head like a mule in a stall, scraping, changing feet" …
  "Yours stood. I'd have said nobody was there, except the floor gave when he stepped to it." / "The rest of them, I can tell you what they
  ate before they came." **The priests' dressing of the answer:** "They put a mountain in it," … "And a sea, and a painted tomb, and
  something to tap your foot to." … "whatever I bring up from down there, they take it and put shoes on it. He said it short and he said it
  plain. Nobody pays to travel down from Thessaly for short and plain." / of the non-Greek word: "Not Greek, so not the god's, says the
  square beard. The smoke talking, or the woman down the hole. The god's been everywhere; he gets about more than they do." / to "before

  Which of those it is, is mine to know." / to silver: "Keep your silver. Whatever's paid on this hill goes to the priests, and I get the
  steps." / to "Was there a day in it?": "You've had your answer to that," (said "watching the crows") "Ask the other." **The WHERE, first
  source (canon):** to "Which city?", the chapter's last line: "Theano shifted on the stone, and grunted with it." / "Pompeii." (no hand on
  a knee). Her house: one swept room, a loom with a brown-and-white striped blanket half woven, a cat asleep "in the warm ash with its paws

#### FELIX — Valens's mule-boy, bought off a Kirrha slaver c. AD 70 aged ~12 and freed with no papers; later sworn to Pompeii's gladiator school (Ch.11–40)
- **Attention / worldview:** fame, fights, who is winning, who is watching. The arena is the most glorious
  thing in the world, and he wants exactly the life that nearly destroyed Valens.
- **Vocabulary band:** fast, boastful street Greek (Part One) that turns into Pompeian Latin slang (Part
  Two); fighters' names and arena terms (thraex, murmillo, retiarius, the palm, the wooden sword). He
  grows from boy to young man (about 21 at the eruption) and the slang matures with him.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** **stacks two or three questions before anyone answers one.** Boasts in
  superlatives. Interrupts himself with a new question.
- **Rhythm:** fast, overlapping, never a pause.
- **Evasion — never says:** that he is afraid of Valens's disapproval; that he is afraid at all; "thank
  you" to Valens.
- **Physicality / silence:** always moving: bouncing on his heels, climbing, leaning. Scratches a tiny palm
  branch on walls he leans against (an action, never a phrase; **used once, Ch.21; Ch.28 is the last
  reservation**). Sleeps anywhere, including against a mule.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by rhythm (stacked questions) and attention (fame and fights)
- **Bleed guard:** no catchphrase and no boast formula repeated; vary the boast every time.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the one who asks three things at once and boasts about all of them, against
  Lucius, who asks one thing gravely and waits for the answer.
- **Sample line:** "Did you see the net? Did you see how he turned it? Is it true you fought at Corinth
  with two cracked fingers and won anyway? Why do I have to hear that from a lanista?"

- **Ch.11 as written (Writer, 2026-10-20; first live appearance. SYNCED to the FINAL page 2026-10-20, after dialogue-polish (every
  burst re-cut for opener variety), hook-craft, the disruptor, continuity repair, polish cycle 1 and finalize line F3; every quote
  below is on the page, checked by script):** **Entry (all four marks):** a voice first ("a boy was telling some animal at the top of
  his voice that it was the worst mule between Parnassus and the sea"); the physical anchor: "The boy had a shovel taller than he
  was. He was a thin one of twelve or so, with straw in his hair." (polish cycle 1 cut the tunic-belt-hair skeleton, the Ch.4
  goat-boy's introduction re-nouned; the knife-cut hair was cut earlier); behavior: "He had me in his eye before I was well through,
  and came straight at me with the shovel."; tension: he wants Valens's approval and will not say so ("Why won't he let me? I know
  poultices. Did he say anything to you about me doing it?"). **Stacked questions, openers rotated (highest two-word frame 2):** "Are
  you Kallia's? You're the one he took up to Pan's in the snow. Did you hit Pan? Which hand? Was there much blood?" (and off "still
  asking, as he went, which hand") / "What's he got in his pouch that ticks? Yours, is it? Each day before he's had his bread he does
  something to it, with his back to me, and if I ask he sends me for water. Does it live? He won't let me near it, and I held a
  fowler's hawk down at the harbor, bare-armed, and it never put a claw in me." / "He doesn't keep things for people," / "Where'd you
  learn leather? Off your father? Had he mules? There was a sailor told me in Syracuse they eat octopus raw. Raw!" / "Chian are
  bigger," / "I never had a Caunian till this winter," / **his own problem, seeded (arena-mad):** "There's boxing at the gymnasium
  before the god sits. A Thessalian, and a man from Elateia who killed somebody at Thebes, they say, with his fists, with one blow.
  Everybody's going. Kallia's lodgers are going. Can I go? I'll have the stalls done before noon." / "It costs you nothing. I'll walk
  there and back, I'll be here before the string is. I'd go a round with the Thessalian myself, if they'd let me in the ring. Have you
  ever seen a man killed with one blow?" / "You've never seen anything." (F3: no tag, no "with great bitterness"; "Felix took himself
  off to fork out the stalls, and forked them so hard that the dog left the yard.") / at the hoof: "Do you want the twitch?" … "I'll
  get the twitch. I'll hold her ear; nobody holds an ear better than me. Or the rope on her hind leg?" / "That's the bad in her,
  coming out?" … "All of it? She'll go to Kirrha tomorrow, won't she?" / the poultice morning: "He was up all night with her. There's
  three sacks gone, and I never heard him once." / to Praxias's quail (the fights axis): "That's the one? From behind the stadium,
  that blinded the Amphissan's bird in one eye? The left, I heard. Did it fight again after, the Amphissan's?" / the report (speed;
  the chapter's one cut-off and its one em-dash): "He went to the wine-seller under the plane tree … and the baker said—" / "The
  square? There's no quails in the square." … "The baker feeds his bird on wine, everybody says so. Wine, to make it brave. Would it
  work on a mule?" / the barred gate: "Who's coming? The Amphissan, about his bird? We've never had it barred in the day, not since I
  came. Is it you?" / "The Amphissan, though?" / from the top of the gate: "Nobody. A cart of oil. Some Thessalians, lost. Nobody. I
  can see clear to the bend from up here, and past it if I stand." / his name: "What's that, writing? A curse? Who's it on? Can you
  write me? Big?" / "Valens! She's written me! Come and see what I look like!" / "Read me," … "Go on, then. Say me out loud." / "He
  can't. Nobody in this yard can but you. Is that one me, with its arms on its hips? Will it wash off, if it rains?" / "Nobody at
  Kirrha's got his name written down. The Cilician called me Boy from Side to Kirrha. Has he told you about the Cilician?" **His
  story, boasted by him (Valens tells none of it):** "He bought me off him on the quay at Kirrha. He paid more for me than he paid for
  the black, and she's four years old and sound, or she was. The Cilician laughed and said nobody had ever paid him so much for a boy
  with a cough. You'd think he hit the Cilician. He never. He just looked at him, and the Cilician gave him a drachma back. You've
  seen how he looks at people." / "The name's his. Felix. It's lucky, in Latin. He talks to the mules in Latin, did you know that?" /
  "He said I could go wherever I liked, and I said where, and he said wherever I liked, and I came here." / "Can I keep it? The dog's
  never seen a name." / to Mara's "Did he take you to the priests," … "and have it cut on the wall?": "What wall?" No paper, no god,
  no wall. His name, ΦΗΛΙΞ, is scratched in capitals on a sherd he keeps. **Four boasts, four shapes (no boast formula):** the
  hawk; the ring; the ear; the bend. **Speed, in his acts and his mouth only:** "Felix did nothing at a walk."; climbs the stable
  rubble to the reeds and drops back down it "though the door was beside him"; eats standing; "he was already on the roof"; "Felix
  was already halfway to the shed"; "Felix had it there, lit."; "Felix left his bucket and went to him."; "The boy was out of the gate
  and after him." (polish cycle 1 removed the three "before [X] had finished" beats; the construction survives once, in the protected

  evening", is "standing square on all four feet, the bad one as well, which she had not done since it went lame, because to take her
  weight off it she would have had to shift, and he was asleep against her." **Knows:** believes Valens cannot read ("He can't. Nobody
  in this yard can but you."); knows the trip up to Pan's and that the watch is Mara's (Mara: "It is mine," … "He is keeping it for
  me."; ENTITY CH11-4); has no word of the notice, the arena or Lupus (Ch.21's lanista is where he hears of Corinth). **Not used, keep
  it so:** the palm-branch scratch (Ch.21, 28, one more if earned); a boast formula used twice; "thank you" to Valens; any
  catchphrase. **WATCH for Ch.12+ (final-page counts):** question openers are rotated (highest two-word frame 2: "Can I…?" 2, "Did
  you/he/it" one each, "Is it you?" 1, "Have you ever…" 1); keep rotating, and give him fewer lines in Ch.12 (he brings the goat home)
  rather than another burst. "already [somewhere]" for his speed: 2, AT CAP. "nobody" in his speech: 6 (WATCH). Exits on a line plus
  a tag and "and" ("He doesn't keep things for people," said Felix, and was gone. / "What wall?" he said, and went out with his
  sherd to show the dog.): 2 after F3, AT CAP; Ch.12 at most 1. The yard dog as his foil: 3 beats; rest it.

#### PLAUTIA — Celer's divorced wife; b. c. AD 44, married to Celer in the autumn of AD 63 at nineteen; the woman Valens was framed with (Ch.16–17, Ch.22)
- **Attention / worldview:** what people want and admire, and what can be given; children (her son
  Marcus, b. autumn AD 64: seven in Ch.16, nine in Ch.22; kept by his father under Roman law). She has learned that everything can be taken, so
  she gives it away first.
- **Vocabulary band:** an aristocrat's exquisite Latin (in Corinth also polished Greek); legal terms used
  correctly (dowry, the *actio rei uxoriae*, guardianship).
- **Syntax fingerprint:** formal, subordinate-clause-heavy sentences **broken by sudden blunt
  questions.** **No contractions.**
- **Rhythm:** a long, beautifully built sentence, then a short question like a slap.
- **Evasion — never says:** anything about the night she was framed; Celer's name, if she can avoid it
  (she says "my former husband").
- **Physicality / silence:** gives away anything anyone admires (the bracelet, a cloak, her lamp), then
  grieves for it in the next room. She is very still in public and veiled in court.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by syntax (formal periods broken by blunt questions) and evasion
  (the night)
- **Bleed guard:** must not take on Celer's warm "we." Her formality is cool and exact, his is warm and
  slippery.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the aristocrat whose perfect Latin cracks into one blunt question, against
  Celer, whose geniality never cracks at all.
- **Sample line:** "My former husband, who keeps my son in a house on the Craneion with a nurse I have
  never been permitted to meet, has asked the court to consider his reputation; do you think the boy
  still knows my face?"
- **Ch.12 (mention only, in Valens's telling; her first naming on the page):** "He wanted a man to walk behind his wife, one that
  people would know from the sand and stand back from. Plautia." Her walks: "To the baths. To her mother's house. Out to Kenchreai, to
  the Egyptian goddess, on her days." At the frame: "She didn't look at me." After: "Her brother took her home," … "Celer kept the
  boy." Her brother "gone to law for her dowry", and his freedman found Valens at the Kirrha harbor. She does not speak and is not
  described; keep her voice and her body for Ch.16. Her sample line's "a house on the Craneion" stays calibration only (continuity
  W-06); Ch.16 must not use it.

#### QUINTUS ARRIUS CELER — legate on the proconsul's staff at Corinth until Nero's grant of freedom (late 67), out of office at the frame (69), back on the restored proconsul's staff by 71–72; the defendant in Rome (Ch.12 by proxy, Ch.17, Ch.22)
- **Attention / worldview:** standing, reputations, who is watching, which way a room leans. Everyone is
  a friend he has not yet needed. Settled by dowry law, never by violence.
- **Vocabulary band:** senatorial Latin worn lightly; easy, social, unhurried.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** genial **first-person plural** ("we," "us," "all of us"), conditionals and soft
  questions that expect agreement. **Uses contractions** and warmth. Never raises his voice.
- **Rhythm:** patient, even, as if there were all the time in the world.
- **Evasion — never says:** the word *wife*. He says "the lady Plautia." He never makes a direct threat
  and never admits a debt.
- **Physicality / silence:** relaxed, smiling, hand on an arm. **Will not walk under ladders or
  scaffolding,** even in a city being rebuilt; his men carry him around it.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by syntax (genial "we," conditionals) and evasion (never "wife,"
  never a threat)
- **Bleed guard:** no villain monologue and no cruelty on the surface.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the only speaker who talks to an enemy as an old friend in the first-person
  plural, against Plautia, who addresses everyone in the second person and in earnest.
- **Sample line:** "Sit, please, both of you; nobody here is in any hurry, and I'd much rather we were
  all friends again by the time the wine comes."
- **Ch.12 by proxy (Writer, 2026-10-20; in Valens's account and in the men he sent. SYNCED to the FINAL page 2026-10-20: every quote
  below is on the page, checked by script):** the man who frames by apology: "He was sorry about it. He said so, more than once, with
  her standing there." "Celer was legate then, on the proconsul's staff."; after the freedom "He'd stayed on at Corinth with nothing to
  be legate of. He had debts. He'd bought a house he couldn't pay for, out where the cypresses are."; the dowry share ("Put a wife away
  for that, and you keep a share of what she brought."); his steward took the tablet; "Celer kept the boy." **His legal claim (W-21;
  see the VALENS card):** not that the freedom went unregistered, but a prior sale: "His story was that he'd bought me from the lanista
  the month before the games, so the lanista had no right to free me, and the magistrate had written down a mistake." In plot terms, a
  backdated bill of sale (not page words). **His men:** a friendly man who was on the benches at Corinth ("I had two drachmas on the
  Gaul.") and knew Lupus by his hand ("you'll know him by his hand"); a big man with "a stick of olive wood"; a third who held Mara
  ("Be still, mistress. Be good."). On the page they carry one knife (the talker's) and one stick, and the third man uses his hands;
  Valens's point is the missing rope: "Those three brought none." **Inference, not page fact:** that they came on the Lechaion boat.
  The page has only "I told them about it the whole crossing." and, at Kirrha that morning, "A boat from Lechaion had come in on the
  morning wind". Two of them got away, and both heard Valens call "Mara." (Ch.17 may use it, or not). Celer himself never appears and
  is never quoted; keep his on-page voice for Ch.17.

#### POMPONIA GRATA — thermopolium keeper on the Via dell'Abbondanza; the family's landlady and neighbor (Ch.19–40)
- **Attention / worldview:** trade, appetite, gossip, her son's election, money that isn't there. Every
  person is a customer, a debtor or a story.
- **Vocabulary band:** rapid Oscan-flavored Pompeian Latin; food, prices of lentils and wine, street
  names, the names of everyone on the block.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** a torrent of comma-spliced clauses, each one a sale or a complaint. **She tells
  you about yourself and never asks a personal question.**
- **Rhythm:** flood, then a command ("Eat this. Hold that." are calibration examples only, never page text; Ch.1's "Eat that," is
  Ch.1's and is never hers).
- **Evasion — never says:** anything that would require asking why. She takes the travel money in Ch.38
  and laughs rather than ask. Her husband's dice debts are mentioned only as a joke.
- **Physicality / silence:** **touches people's arms** while she talks. Whitewashes rivals' election
  notices at night, personally. Rests her forearms on the counter over the steaming pots.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by syntax (telling, never asking) and physicality (touch)
- **Bleed guard:** must not ask questions the way Felix does, and must not take on Kallia's terse
  imperatives as a rhythm. Grata's commands come at the end of a flood.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the woman who narrates you to your face and never asks you a thing, against
  Kallia, who says almost nothing, and Felix, who only asks.
- **Sample line:** "That pot isn't worth the glue and you know it and you'll mend it anyway, that's your
  trouble, you'd mend a cracked egg if somebody cried over it. Here. Hold this, it's hot."

## THE CHILDREN

#### LUCIUS — son of Mara and Valens; b. summer AD 74 (born on the page Ch.24; in arms Ch.25; speaks Ch.27–29, 32, 34, 37–44; age 5 at the eruption)
- **Attention / worldview:** rules and real tasks. He wants to be given a job and takes adults at their
  word. He is Valens's stillness without the fear.
- **Vocabulary band:** Latin first, some Greek from his parents, a few English words from Mara. He calls
  Valens **Tata** (the Latin nursery word for father, made clear by context once) and Mara **Mama**.
- **Age-stage voice:**
  - **About 2 (Ch.27–29):** single words and two-word requests; names objects; watches.
  - **3 (Ch.32):** fever; mostly sound and a few words; a short sentence on waking.
  - **4 (Ch.34):** short whole sentences; questions about how things work and what is allowed.
  - **5 (Ch.37–44):** full sentences, careful and literal. He acts on instructions exactly as given and
    asks one grave question at a time.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** complete, careful sentences; statements of fact; one question, then waiting.
- **Rhythm:** slow and considered for a child; long silences while he watches.
- **Evasion — never says:** that he is frightened. He asks what to do instead. He never whines.
- **Physicality / silence:** still, watchful; the knucklebone rolled and caught; holds a lamp with both
  hands when trusted with it.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (rules and tasks) and rhythm (one grave question,
  then waiting)
- **Bleed guard:** must not quote instructions back as a habit. His literalism shows in what he does, not
  in a repeated verbal form.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the child who asks one serious question and waits, against Aelia, who never
  waits for anything.
- **Sample line (age 5):** "Tata said I could carry the lamp if I walk. I'm walking."

## THE 1998 FRAME

#### EMILIO REYES — Mara's father; field archaeologist, Philadelphia; d. January 1998 aged 68 (Ch.1 outgoing message on tape; past-facing memory throughout)
- **Attention / worldview:** places and strata, meaning where a thing was found and how deep. He locates
  himself and everyone else by *where*. The past was more vivid to him than the people waiting at home.
- **Vocabulary band:** a warm, performing university man's American English; field slang; place names.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** easy, generous, a little theatrical, a speaker used to rooms of students.
  Promises put in the conditional and the season, never the date.
- **Rhythm:** a cheerful run that ends on an invitation.
- **Evasion — never says:** **when** he will be back. He never names a date (contrast Fenn, who names
  dates wrongly). His promise to take her ("next season, you come with me") may be quoted verbatim **once
  in the whole book**; everywhere else it is paraphrased (at-risk list).
- **Physicality / silence:** absent; known by objects (the 1966 Seiko stopped on the nightstand, the
  Pentax, the field notebooks she does not open, the dig slides, the answering machine).
- **Canon guard (foundation §3; synced 2026-10-19 after Ch.7 C-01):** he **never took her abroad**, not once.
  She knows his sites (Sicily, Syracuse, Cyprus) only from his slides and his talk at the kitchen table (Ch.1;
  Ch.7 "from his slides"). No later chapter may give her a trip with him, at any age.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by evasion (never commits to a when) and attention (where)
- **Bleed guard:** Mara's memories of him must not develop a recurring framing line ("My father used to
  say…"). Vary the entry every time.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the man who tells you where he is and never when he'll be back, against Fenn,
  who tells you exactly when he'll be back and is wrong.
- **Sample line (the tape):** "You've got the Reyes house. I'm out in the field, or I'm asleep in the
  chair, and either way leave me your name and I'll call you when I'm back."

#### PROF. HALLORAN — Emilio's permit contact and colleague, phoning from Naples (Ch.1 on the machine; Ch.2 by phone)
- **Attention / worldview:** paperwork, deadlines, permits, the season's logistics, the Soprintendenza.
  Kind in the way institutions are kind.
- **Vocabulary band:** Irish-born academic long resident in Naples; administrative English with Italian
  office words ("the Soprintendenza," "the *permesso*").
- **Syntax fingerprint:** apology, then request; euphemism around death; dates and deadlines given
  precisely.
- **Rhythm:** courteous, slightly over-long, trailing into "well."
- **Evasion — never says:** "died" or "dead." He says "in Emilio's place" and "since January." There is
  **no portent** in his Campanian invitation; it is a neutral fact.
- **Physicality / silence:** a voice on a bad international line; the pause before a hard word.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by evasion (euphemism for death) and attention (paperwork and dates)
- **Bleed guard:** no hint of destiny or of Pompeii as meaningful. He is a man with forms.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the only voice that wraps death in paperwork, against Emilio's tape, which
  is all warmth and no dates.
- **Sample line:** "I'm sorry to ring about forms at a time like this, Ms. Reyes, but the permit needs a
  name on it by the twentieth of April, and your father's is, well. It's still the one on it."
- **Ch.2 as written (Writer, 2026-10-18):** rings the house on the last Saturday in March (~10 a.m.
  Philadelphia / 4 p.m. Naples, both still on standard time); the machine "only beeps" (no greeting since
  Ch.1). His own life on the call: he and his wife are leaving their flat after thirty-one years; he sits on
  the floor of an emptied room with the telephone in his lap; the new tenants arrive to measure for
  curtains. The Soprintendenza accept him as director but returned the cession marked *firma mancante*
  (the outgoing director's signature missing); Mara signs an heir's declaration before a notary instead
  (by the fifteenth; the 20th is a Monday). Asks for Emilio's last-season field notebooks (the north
  transects exist only there) "by the end of June". Invites her for the season from 6 July "in Emilio's
  place"; she says she might be in Greece; "you'll practically be next door." Never says "died." Speaks
  Italian to the tenants, not cheerfully.

#### IRENE SZABO — antiques dealer, Pine Street's Antique Row; Hungarian, in her seventies (Ch.1)
- **Attention / worldview:** authenticity: fakes, period accuracy, what a thing will fetch, whether a
  customer is a dealer or a fool. She bought the map only because it is *right* for its period.
- **Vocabulary band:** precise immigrant English with dealer's terms (lot, provenance, estate sale,
  laid paper). Sparing.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** **no contractions;** short present-tense verdicts; statements where others
  would ask questions ("You are not a dealer.").
- **Rhythm:** a verdict, a pause, a price.
- **Evasion — never says:** condolences, sentiment, or any warning or destiny line about the map.
- **Physicality / silence:** looks over glasses she is not wearing; weights a chart's corners with
  whatever is to hand; haggles without moving.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by syntax (no contractions, verdicts) and attention (authenticity)
- **Bleed guard:** must not become the mysterious shopkeeper; she wants it off her shelves.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the seller who sells by contempt in very few words, against Grata, who sells
  by flood and flattery.
- **Sample line:** "Fakers make the mountains too tall. They think tall looks old. This one is dull in the
  right places, which is why I paid for it."
- **Ch.1 as written (Writer, 2026-10-18):** buzzer-and-speaker shop door; magnifier pushed up into her
  white braid; liver-colored cardigan, fingerless gloves; a mute TV with a college game and a $5 bet with
  the barber next door (her own life, nothing to do with Mara). Notices the obituary name ("There was a
  Reyes in the *Inquirer*") and lets Mara's "It's a common name" stand. No condolence, no warning.

#### DOUG FESSLER — field archaeologist; dug with Emilio eleven seasons in Cyprus and two in Sicily; gave the eulogy (Ch.1)
- **Attention / worldview:** his own fieldwork and its logistics: his lost duffel, his context sheets,
  the sherd he could not place in 1984. Grief reaches him as anecdote about a site, never as a feeling
  stated.
- **Vocabulary band:** American field-archaeologist shop talk (context sheets, type series, section,
  offprints, dig house), plain and warm.
- **Syntax fingerprint:** runaway anecdote that loops back to correct itself; agrees with himself out loud;
  talks around food in his mouth.
- **Rhythm:** a story, a self-interruption, an offer of practical help ("I can do the office").
- **Evasion — never says:** "died," or anything about his own grief; he cuts the story he would have cried
  at and says so instead of crying.
- **Physicality / silence:** a fresh winter-season sunburn from Jordan with a hat-line across the forehead
  and peeling at the nose; a borrowed tie; a paper plate holding one stick of celery, which he talks to.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (his own site logistics) and physicality (the sunburn)
- **Bleed guard:** must not notice materials or joins (Mara's axis); his sherd talk is about *placing* a
  thing in a sequence, never about how it was made or mended.
- **Chaos on the page (subjects, never phrases):** Royal Jordanian lost his duffel with six weeks of context
  sheets; he cannot stop talking about it at a memorial.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the colleague who mourns through his own anecdotes and luggage, against
  Halloran, who mourns through permits and dates.
- **Sample line:** "Don't look at the nose. Six weeks in a hat and the one day I take it off they're
  pouring concrete."

#### GLORIA — Mara's cousin on her father's side; ~36 in 1998; married to Ray, fourteen years (Ch.1)
- **Attention / worldview:** the family's practical ledger: leftovers, freezers, keys, who called whom,
  who was offended and who had to lie down. She manages grief by assigning errands.
- **Vocabulary band:** Philadelphia family English, quick and contracted, with an occasional Spanish
  kinship word (*Tía*).
- **Syntax fingerprint:** short logistical questions ("Where'd you go?" "How much?" "Did you eat
  anything?") followed by instructions; tells you her own small humiliations as comedy.
- **Rhythm:** a complaint about herself, a question, a list of jobs, a command.
- **Evasion — never says:** Emilio's name. In Ch.1 he is only "him," "his machine," "nobody gets him."
  She never asks Mara how she feels.
- **Physicality / silence:** works with her hands while she talks (foil folded with the heel of the hand),
  stockinged feet with her pumps parked under the coat rack; the long wordless look (Ch.1), held instead of
  a sentence; holds a coat open at a child's height.
- **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by evasion (never names the dead man) and attention (errands and
  the family ledger)
- **Bleed guard:** never Mara's dry aside or her eye for materials; never Grata's flattery or sales talk
  (Gloria asks practical questions; Grata never asks). Her hands-at-work is *domestic packing* only, to stay
  clear of Kallia's labor-attention in Delphi.
- **Chaos on the page (subjects, never phrases):** wore two different earrings (a pearl stud and a gold
  hoop) through the whole memorial; Ray called it a style.
- **DISTINCTNESS GUARANTEE:** the relative who will not say the dead man's name and hands you a job
  instead, against Halloran, who says the name and wraps the death in paperwork.
- **Sample line:** "Your keys are in the freezer door, don't ask me why, and Ray's waiting, so take the
  pierogi."

#### Ch.4 unnamed walk-on and mention-only names (no card needed unless he returns or is named)
- **The goat-boy** (Corycian slope, autumn AD 70; UNNAMED: Mara asks his name and he answers with
  hers). About nine; brown coarse tunic belted with cord; bare feet gray with dust, soles hard as
  saddle leather; a sling round his neck, pouch on his chest; hair knife-cropped; a crust under his
  nose; a stick he keeps low; a black-handled leather bag (white cheese and a heel of barley bread
  in a gray rag). **Attention:** goddess or trouble, then his goats, his thorn, and the shiny thing.
  **Syntax:** rural Phocian Koine rendered in short transliterated bursts (*Ti? Pothen ílthes? Ek
  tou antrou? Móni í? Mí gráfe. Ti dósis? Pheu. Phage. Kalon. Ide. Katō. Makran. Késar en Rómi*),
  imperatives and questions, never a full sentence Mara can follow. Shifted vowels are spelled as
  sound (eta/ei/oi → i, ai → e, upsilon → ü); Mara decodes those words only from gesture or context.
  The word-doubling cadence is HIS alone (Mara's echoes were cut in cycle 1). **Evasion:** his own
  name. **Physicality:** spits into the neck of his tunic against the uncanny (once); rubs out her
  written ΔΕΛΦΟΙ with his foot; laughs in high hiccups when she takes *nümfi* for his name; spits out the granola bar; keeps the
  foil wrapper down his tunic; digs a thorn out of his heel with another thorn while grumbling at a
  goat called Kissa. Says *nymphē* three times (rendered "Nümfi" twice, "Nymphē" on the third, when
  Mara hears it). **Verbal tic:** none — distinguished by attention (the uncanny vs. the practical
  goatherd's day) and physicality. No device; he notices no materials or joins. **DISTINCTNESS
  GUARANTEE:** the only speaker in the book whose words reach the page as sound Mara cannot parse,
  against the 1998 goatherd (Ch.3), who speaks one word of modern Greek she understands at once.
  Different century, different person. (If he is ever named, promote to a full card.)
- **Mentioned by name only:** Kleodamos (on the page twice, ¶49 and ¶55: the boy's answer to "who is
  archon": a Delphic eponymous archon, fictional, meaningless to Mara; NOT a year-dating clue; not the
  pen's owner and not the boy's father); the month Boathoos (Delphic,
  roughly Sept–Oct; Mara does not know the Delphic calendar's correlation); Kissa (a goat).
- **Spent in Ch.4 (do not reuse):** "Khaire/Khére" farce; the Theophrastus superstitious-man
  aside; "strangers and beggars are from Zeus" (Odyssey, quoted once); the Wawa hoagie case.

#### Ch.6 unnamed walk-ons and mention-only names (no card needed unless they return or are named)
*(Synced to the final page 2026-10-19, after dialogue-polish, disruptor, continuity repair and polish cycle 1.)*
- **The charcoal burner** (top of the cliff path above Delphi, November AD 70): the man with the donkey Valens
  suspects on the way up; that evening he sits up with his kiln (a long hump of earth and turf, smoke seeping from
  every seam) on an upturned basket with a sack across his head and shoulders. Hails them once as "Mule-man!"
  (one use only, so it is not an epithet): "Come and warm yourselves. She won't mind." **His own life:** the kiln,
  nine days burning ("Nine days she's been at it, and now this."), which he talks to as "she"/"girl" ("Easy, girl.
  Hold it in.") and stamps shut where flame shows; a grievance about the god's oxen that runs past Mara ("Did you
  get any of the god's ox?" The rest ran on past me. I caught the number four in it, and the council, and a
  grievance about meat.); to Valens's "I was at Kirrha": "So you ate what we ate. Smoke." Roasts chestnuts at the
  edge of the embers and pushes them to Mara with his foot ("Eat. They're split already."). His cousin's boy is
  the Ch.4 goat-boy, who saw her "step out of Pan's cave at the olive beating"; he says the next part slowly, to
  her ("The boy says you ate his cheese and paid him in a cake made of hay."), which is why she can answer "It was
  oats"; "It's all hay to a boy." Fast mountain Greek: "I lost words out of everything he said, and none of
  Valens's answers." At "She hit Pan" the sack across his shoulders shakes (no laugh line, no bodily aftermath;
  the donkey opens its eyes and shuts them again). "Sleep here by her. You'll not get down in the dark." No
  device; notices no materials.
- **A Theban on Kallia's gallery** ("Kallia! Are those lentils ever coming?").
- **Mention only:** the temple painter the priests hang off the roof each spring "with a pot of red" (came off the

  storm were CUT from Ch.6, AUTHOR-CP2-2, 2026-10-19; neither is on the page);
  Gloria, unnamed as "a cousin", in Mara's cliff speech (the pearl in one ear and the gold hoop in the other

- **Mules (no names by design):** the gray (the lead; Mara rides her and is towed up the cliff by her tail), the

#### Ch.9 unnamed walk-ons and mention-only names (no card needed unless they return or are named)
